summary: Specifies the Russian Dolls bandwidth constraints model for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering. In this model, limits are nested so that each traffic class sits inside a larger allowance, like nested dolls. This is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Russian nesting dolls fit one inside another. This memo describes a way to share network capacity where each smaller group of traffic fits inside a bigger group's limit.

subtitle: Nested bandwidth constraints for quality-of-service traffic engineering

tldr.problem: Networks need to allocate bandwidth fairly among different classes of traffic while maintaining quality of service. Simple bandwidth sharing mechanisms do not provide adequate control over how much bandwidth each traffic class receives.
tldr.mechanism: The Russian Dolls Model (RDM) defines nested bandwidth constraints where each traffic class sits inside a larger constraint, like nesting dolls. Lower-numbered classes include higher-numbered classes within their limits, ensuring predictable bandwidth allocation across multiple priorities.
tldr.outcome: RDM allows networks to enforce bandwidth isolation across traffic classes, maintain efficiency, and protect against quality degradation without requiring complex protocols. It is simple to implement and works well with preemption-based priority schemes.

today: RFC 4127 is an experimental specification. It defines the Russian Dolls Model as one approach to DS-TE bandwidth constraints. While experimental, RDM has been implemented in various MPLS systems and is used in networks where traffic classes need different bandwidth guarantees.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Russian Dolls Model (RDM) is one approach to implementing Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE), which allows networks to enforce different bandwidth constraints for different classes of traffic. This document provides a detailed specification of RDM, which is also supported by the protocol extensions defined in RFC 4124.

RDM is designed to address the fundamental requirement of being able to enforce different bandwidth constraints for different traffic classes in a network. Rather than treating all traffic equally, RDM allows a network administrator to specify how much bandwidth different classes of traffic (such as voice, premium data, and best-effort data) can use on each link.
sections.plainLanguage: This defines one model for how network routers can decide how much capacity to reserve for voice, premium data, and regular data so each gets what it needs.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
RDM uses two main concepts: Class-Types (CTs) and TE-Classes. A Class-Type is a set of traffic trunks that shares a specific set of bandwidth constraints. A given traffic tunnel belongs to the same Class-Type on all links it crosses. A TE-Class combines a Class-Type with a preemption priority level, allowing high-priority traffic of one class to bump lower-priority traffic of other classes.

RDM also defines Reserved(CTc) as the total bandwidth reserved by all established label switched paths (LSPs) that belong to a given Class-Type. The model is compatible with bandwidth-sharing mechanisms like Shared Mesh Restoration, which allows backup LSPs to share bandwidth across multiple primary LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each type of traffic (voice, data, best-effort) gets its own label. You can also add a priority number so urgent traffic can push aside less important traffic to get through.

sections.title: The Russian Dolls Model Defined
sections.content:
The Russian Dolls Model is defined with these core rules: there are at most 8 Class-Types (numbered 0 through 7) and 8 corresponding Bandwidth Constraints (BC0 through BC7). For each Class-Type c, the sum of all traffic in Class-Type c and all higher-numbered Class-Types MUST NOT exceed BCc. In other words, BC0 (the sum of all classes 0 through 7) is the largest constraint, BC1 (classes 1 through 7) is smaller, and so on.

This creates a hierarchy where: All LSPs from CT7 use no more than BC7. All LSPs from CT6 and CT7 together use no more than BC6. All LSPs from CT5, CT6, and CT7 together use no more than BC5. And so on, with all classes combined using no more than BC0, which equals the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth.

Both preemption within a Class-Type and across Class-Types is allowed, making it possible to enforce strict isolation across classes when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine the largest constraint (BC0) as the biggest doll. Inside it is BC1, which limits voice and premium data. Inside that is BC2 for just voice. Each constraint works like a maximum limit for everything at that level and above.

sections.title: Practical Examples
sections.content:
Consider a simple network with two traffic classes. An administrator might configure: Voice (CT1) limited to 1.5 Gb/s (BC1 = 1.5 Gb/s) and Voice plus Data (CT0+CT1) limited to the full 2.5 Gb/s link capacity (BC0 = 2.5 Gb/s). This ensures voice traffic never exceeds 1.5 Gb/s while data can use up to 1 Gb/s of the remaining capacity.

A more complex example with three classes might use: Voice at 45% of link capacity (BC2), Premium Data plus Voice at 80% (BC1), and all classes at 100% (BC0). By assigning preemption priorities (voice with priority 0, premium data with priority 1, best-effort with priority 2), the network ensures voice traffic can preempt premium data, which can preempt best-effort traffic, while the bandwidth constraints guarantee each class gets an appropriate share.
sections.plainLanguage: You could say voice gets 1.5 Gb/s, and voice-plus-data gets 2.5 Gb/s total. Then data automatically gets the leftover 1 Gb/s. If needed, voice can bump data off the network to guarantee quality.

sections.title: Advantages and Deployment
sections.content:
RDM is attractive because it is relatively simple to understand and implement compared to more flexible models. The model can ensure bandwidth efficiency while protecting all traffic classes against quality degradation, even when preemption is used. When preemption is enabled, RDM simultaneously achieves isolation across Class-Types, bandwidth efficiency, and protection against QoS degradation.

RDM only requires limited protocol extensions, making it practical to deploy. However, without preemption enabled, RDM can still ensure bandwidth efficiency and QoS protection but cannot guarantee strict isolation between classes. The model assigns IANA Bandwidth Constraints Model ID 0 to RDM.
sections.plainLanguage: This model is popular because it is not too complicated, but gives networks good control over quality. It works especially well when you let important traffic interrupt regular traffic to get through.
